title: Modern NLP & Practical Considerations
description: A preview of contextual embeddings and the Transformer era, how to evaluate generative NLP models honestly, handling messy real-world and multilingual text, and the ethical considerations every NLP practitioner should know.

lessons.title: From Static to Contextual Embeddings
lessons.description: See the natural next step beyond Word2Vec and GloVe — and get a preview of where NLP is headed next.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what a contextual embedding is and why it solves a key limitation of static embeddings.

sections.title: 🔁 A quick recap of the limitation
sections.content: Recall from module 2: Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText all produce **static embeddings** — one fixed vector per word, no matter the context. "Bank" gets the exact same vector whether it means a riverbank or a financial institution — a real limitation for genuinely understanding language.

sections.title: 🌊 Contextual embeddings: a different vector for every context
sections.content:
**Contextual embeddings** solve this by producing a *different* vector for a word depending on the specific sentence it appears in — computed by a model that reads the entire surrounding sentence (or passage) before deciding on that word's representation for this particular occurrence.

```
"I deposited money at the bank"        → "bank" vector reflects financial meaning
"I sat by the river bank"               → "bank" vector reflects the riverside meaning
# Two different vectors for the same word, based on context
```

This is a genuinely different, more powerful kind of representation than anything in module 2 — meaning is no longer looked up per-word from a fixed table, but computed fresh, in context, every single time.

sections.title: 🚀 A preview of what's coming
sections.content:
Modern contextual embedding models — like BERT and its many variants — are built on the **Transformer** architecture, using the attention mechanism from module 3, scaled up dramatically and trained on massive amounts of text. These models represented a major leap in NLP capability when introduced, and remain foundational to most modern NLP systems and large language models today.

This course has built up every piece needed to understand why this works: tokenization, embeddings, sequence models, attention — a dedicated later course goes deep into the Transformer architecture itself, and another covers the large language models built on top of it.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) are now useless.** They remain fast, lightweight, and genuinely useful for simpler tasks or resource-constrained settings — contextual embeddings are more powerful but also far more computationally expensive.

**Underestimating how big a shift this represents.** Moving from "one fixed vector per word" to "a vector computed fresh from context every time" is a fundamentally different, more expressive way of representing meaning — not just an incremental tweak.

**Expecting to fully understand contextual embeddings without the Transformer architecture behind them.** This lesson is intentionally a preview — the full mechanics are the subject of a dedicated later course, once attention (from module 3) has had time to sink in.

questions.question: What is the key difference between static embeddings and contextual embeddings?
options: Static embeddings are always more accurate than contextual ones
Static embeddings assign one fixed vector per word regardless of context; contextual embeddings compute a different vector depending on the surrounding sentence
Contextual embeddings don't use any numerical vectors at all
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explanation: Static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText) give every occurrence of a word the same vector; contextual embeddings compute a fresh representation based on the specific sentence the word appears in, capturing context-dependent meaning.

questions.question: How does a contextual embedding model handle a word like 'bank' that has multiple meanings?
options: It always picks the most common meaning and ignores context
It produces a different vector for 'bank' depending on the surrounding context, reflecting which meaning is actually intended in that specific sentence
It refuses to process ambiguous words at all
It removes ambiguous words from the input entirely
questions.explanation: Because contextual embeddings are computed fresh from the surrounding text each time, a word like 'bank' gets a vector that reflects its riverbank meaning in one sentence and its financial meaning in another — directly solving the ambiguity problem static embeddings couldn't address.

questions.question: What architecture are modern contextual embedding models like BERT built on?
options: Bag of words
The Transformer architecture, using the attention mechanism
A single perceptron
Basic TF-IDF vectorization
questions.explanation: Modern contextual embedding models are built on the Transformer architecture, which scales up the attention mechanism introduced earlier in this course — the full details of this architecture are covered in a dedicated later course.

questions.question: What key limitation of static embeddings do contextual embeddings address?
options: Static embeddings require too much storage space
Static embeddings give the same vector to a word regardless of its meaning in a specific context
Static embeddings cannot be computed for any language
Static embeddings don't use numerical vectors at all
questions.explanation: Contextual embeddings solve the problem that static embeddings assign one fixed vector per word no matter the context, which fails to capture context-dependent meaning like 'bank'.

questions.question: How is a contextual embedding for a word computed?
options: By looking it up in a fixed table, exactly like a static embedding
By a model that reads the entire surrounding sentence or passage before deciding on that word's representation for this occurrence
Randomly, with no relationship to context
By counting how many times the word appears in the corpus
questions.explanation: Contextual embeddings are computed fresh, based on the specific sentence or passage the word appears in, rather than looked up from a static per-word table.

questions.question: What architecture underlies modern contextual embedding models like BERT?
options: Bag of words
The Transformer architecture, built on the attention mechanism
Basic stemming and lemmatization rules
K-means clustering
questions.explanation: Modern contextual embedding models like BERT are built on the Transformer architecture, scaling up the attention mechanism introduced earlier in the course.

questions.question: Does the lesson suggest static embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe are now completely useless?
options: Yes, they should never be used again
No — they remain fast, lightweight, and useful for simpler tasks or resource-constrained settings
Static embeddings were never actually useful at all
Static embeddings and contextual embeddings are identical in every way
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns against assuming static embeddings are now useless — they remain practical for simpler tasks or when computational resources are limited.

questions.question: According to the lesson, is this contextual embeddings lesson meant to be a full technical treatment of the Transformer architecture?
options: Yes, it covers every mechanical detail
No — it's intentionally a preview, with the full mechanics covered in a dedicated later course
The Transformer architecture is not related to contextual embeddings at all
This lesson replaces the need for any further study of Transformers
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly frames itself as a preview, noting that the full mechanics of the Transformer architecture are covered in a dedicated later course.

lessons.title: Evaluating NLP Models
lessons.description: Learn the specialized metrics needed for generation tasks, where a single 'right answer' doesn't exist.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe how BLEU, ROUGE, and perplexity are used to evaluate different kinds of NLP models.

sections.title: 🔁 When classification metrics still apply
sections.content: For classification-style NLP tasks — sentiment analysis, NER (framed as sequence labeling), topic classification — the metrics from the machine learning course apply directly: accuracy, precision, recall, F1. Nothing new is needed there.

sections.title: 🌍 BLEU: for translation
sections.content:
**BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy)** measures how much a generated translation overlaps with one or more human reference translations, based primarily on matching n-grams (recall n-grams from module 1) between the generated text and the reference(s).

```
Generated: "the cat sat on the mat"
Reference: "the cat is sitting on the mat"
# BLEU compares n-gram overlap between the two
```

Higher BLEU generally indicates a translation closer to the reference(s) — but since multiple valid translations of the same sentence can exist (as covered in module 3), BLEU is an imperfect, if very widely used, proxy for translation quality.

sections.title: 📝 ROUGE: for summarization
sections.content: **ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation)** is conceptually similar to BLEU but tuned for summarization — it measures how much of the important content from a reference summary is captured (overlap-based, similar n-gram matching logic, with a few different specific variants) by the generated summary.

sections.title: 🎲 Perplexity: for language models
sections.content:
**Perplexity** measures how "surprised" a language model is by real text — essentially, how well it predicts the actual next words in genuine held-out text. Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the text that actually occurred, indicating it's a better fit for that kind of language.

```
# Conceptual intuition
# Low perplexity  → the model consistently expects roughly what actually appears next
# High perplexity → the model is frequently "surprised" by the actual next word
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating BLEU or ROUGE scores as a perfect measure of quality.** Both are overlap-based proxies — a genuinely excellent alternative phrasing can still score lower simply for not matching the specific reference text's exact wording.

**Using perplexity to compare models trained on very different text or vocabularies.** Perplexity values aren't directly comparable across different tokenizations, vocabularies, or datasets — comparisons are only meaningful under matched conditions.

**Relying on automated metrics alone for high-stakes generation tasks.** Human evaluation remains important for catching real quality issues (factual errors, awkward phrasing, hallucination) that overlap-based automatic metrics can miss entirely.

questions.question: What does BLEU score primarily measure?
options: How fast a translation model runs
How much a generated translation overlaps (largely via n-gram matching) with one or more human reference translations
The exact grammatical correctness of a sentence
The number of words in the generated translation
questions.explanation: BLEU compares the generated translation's n-grams against those of reference translation(s), using that overlap as a proxy for translation quality — higher overlap generally suggests closer alignment with the reference.

questions.question: What does a lower perplexity score indicate about a language model?
options: The model performs worse and is more confused by the text
The model is less 'surprised' by the actual text — it assigns higher probability to what genuinely comes next, indicating a better fit
The model has fewer parameters
The model was trained on less data
questions.explanation: Perplexity measures how well a language model predicts real text — lower perplexity means the model's predictions align well with what actually occurs, indicating it has learned the patterns of that kind of language effectively.

questions.question: Why can BLEU or ROUGE penalize a genuinely excellent translation or summary unfairly?
options: These metrics are always perfectly accurate with no flaws
Both are overlap-based against specific reference text, so a valid alternative phrasing that doesn't closely match the reference's exact wording can still score low
BLEU and ROUGE only work for very short texts
These metrics cannot be computed automatically
questions.explanation: Since BLEU and ROUGE fundamentally measure textual overlap with a specific reference, a high-quality output phrased differently from that particular reference can receive a misleadingly low score, despite being a genuinely good translation or summary.

questions.question: For classification-style NLP tasks like sentiment analysis, which metrics apply directly?
options: Only BLEU and ROUGE
Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 from the machine learning course
Only perplexity
No standard metrics exist for these tasks
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that classification-style tasks can use the same metrics from the machine learning course — accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 — directly, without needing specialized generation metrics.

questions.question: What does BLEU primarily rely on to compare a generated translation to reference translations?
options: Character count differences
N-gram matching/overlap
Random sampling of words
The total file size of the text
questions.explanation: BLEU compares n-grams (recall n-grams from module 1) between the generated text and reference translations to compute an overlap-based score.

questions.question: What is ROUGE tuned for, compared to BLEU?
options: Machine translation specifically
Summarization, measuring how much important content from a reference summary is captured
Speech recognition accuracy
Named entity recognition performance
questions.explanation: ROUGE is conceptually similar to BLEU but is specifically tuned for evaluating summarization, measuring how well a generated summary captures a reference summary's important content.

questions.question: Why can't perplexity values be directly compared across models trained on very different datasets?
options: Perplexity is always exactly the same for every model
Perplexity values aren't directly comparable across different tokenizations, vocabularies, or datasets
Perplexity can only be computed for translation tasks
Comparing perplexity across datasets is always valid and meaningful
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that perplexity comparisons are only meaningful under matched conditions — different tokenizations, vocabularies, or datasets make direct comparisons unreliable.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend human evaluation alongside automated metrics for high-stakes generation tasks?
options: Automated metrics are always perfectly sufficient on their own
Human evaluation can catch real quality issues like factual errors or hallucination that overlap-based automatic metrics can miss entirely
Human evaluation is never useful for NLP tasks
BLEU and ROUGE already guarantee perfect quality assessment
questions.explanation: Since automated overlap-based metrics can miss issues like factual errors or hallucination, human evaluation remains an important complement for assessing generation quality in high-stakes settings.

lessons.title: Handling Multilingual and Real-World Text
lessons.description: Learn the practical, messy realities of working with text outside of clean textbook examples.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can list common real-world text challenges and describe practical strategies for handling them.

sections.title: 🌍 Multilingual text
sections.content: Real-world applications often need to handle multiple languages, which raises practical questions: does one model need to handle every language, or should you train/use a separate model per language? Modern multilingual models (many contextual embedding models have multilingual variants) can handle many languages within a single model, though performance can vary significantly across languages, generally correlating with how much training data existed for each one — lower-resource languages tend to see noticeably weaker performance.

sections.title: 🗑️ Noisy, informal text
sections.content: Real text — social media posts, chat messages, customer support tickets — is far messier than the clean, well-formatted examples in a textbook: typos, inconsistent capitalization, emojis, slang, abbreviations ("ur", "lol", "brb"), and code-switching (mixing multiple languages within a single message) are all common. Models trained primarily on clean, formal text (like news articles) can perform noticeably worse on this kind of messier, informal real-world text unless they've specifically seen similar examples during training.

sections.title: 🛠️ Practical strategies
sections.content:
• **Match training data to deployment conditions** — if your model will process casual social media text, ideally train (or at least evaluate) on similarly casual, informal text, not just clean formal writing
• **Robust tokenization** — subword tokenization (module 0) helps gracefully handle typos and unusual words better than pure word-level tokenization
• **Preprocessing choices matter more here** — decisions like whether to lowercase everything, how to handle emojis, and whether to expand abbreviations can meaningfully affect performance on noisy text
• **Test on realistic, representative examples** — not just clean textbook-style sentences — before trusting a model's real-world performance

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Evaluating a model only on clean, well-formatted test examples.** This can badly overestimate how well it will actually perform on the messier, more realistic text it will encounter in production.

**Assuming a single multilingual model performs equally well across every language it supports.** Performance often varies significantly, generally tracking how much training data was available for each specific language.

**Underestimating how much preprocessing choices affect noisy text specifically.** Decisions that barely matter on clean text (like exact capitalization handling) can have an outsized effect on messy, informal real-world text.

questions.question: Why might a multilingual NLP model perform noticeably worse on some languages than others?
options: Multilingual models can only ever support exactly two languages
Performance often correlates with how much training data was available for each specific language — lower-resource languages tend to see weaker performance
All languages are always handled with exactly equal performance
Multilingual models cannot process any language at all
questions.explanation: Since models learn patterns from their training data, languages with less available training data (lower-resource languages) typically see weaker performance than languages that were well-represented during training.

questions.question: Why might a model trained only on clean, formal news articles perform poorly on social media text?
options: Social media text and news articles are actually identical in style
Social media text is far messier — typos, slang, emojis, and abbreviations differ significantly from the clean, formal patterns the model learned during training
Models cannot process any text with emojis under any circumstances
This performance gap never actually occurs in practice
questions.explanation: A model's learned patterns reflect its training data — a model trained exclusively on clean, formal text hasn't been exposed to the informal patterns (slang, typos, abbreviations) common in social media, so it often struggles when applied to that very different style of text.

questions.question: Why is it important to test an NLP model on realistic, representative examples rather than only clean textbook-style sentences?
options: Testing on clean examples always perfectly predicts real-world performance
Evaluating only on clean examples can significantly overestimate how well a model will actually perform on the messier, more varied text it will encounter in real deployment
Realistic examples are always easier for a model to process than clean ones
Testing methodology has no effect on how well results reflect real-world performance
questions.explanation: Real-world text is often much messier than clean, well-formatted test examples — evaluating only on the latter can give a misleadingly optimistic picture of how a model will actually perform once deployed on genuine, more varied text.

questions.question: What factor does the lesson say multilingual model performance generally correlates with?
options: The alphabetical order of the language's name
How much training data existed for each specific language
The number of vowels in the language
The geographic size of the country where the language is spoken
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that multilingual model performance generally correlates with how much training data existed for each language, with lower-resource languages seeing weaker performance.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a common feature of noisy, informal real-world text?
options: Perfectly consistent capitalization
Typos, emojis, slang, and abbreviations like 'ur' or 'lol'
Exclusively formal, grammatically perfect sentences
A complete absence of any punctuation errors
questions.explanation: The lesson lists typos, inconsistent capitalization, emojis, slang, and abbreviations as common features of messy, informal real-world text like social media posts.

questions.question: What does 'code-switching' refer to in the context of real-world text?
options: Switching between different programming languages
Mixing multiple languages within a single message
Changing font styles mid-sentence
Switching between uppercase and lowercase randomly
questions.explanation: Code-switching refers to mixing multiple languages within a single message or conversation, which is common in real-world multilingual communication.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend matching training data to deployment conditions?
options: Training data never needs to resemble deployment data
A model intended for casual social media text should ideally be trained or evaluated on similarly casual text, not just clean formal writing
Deployment conditions are always identical to training conditions by default
Matching training data to deployment conditions has no effect on performance
questions.explanation: If a model will process casual, informal text in deployment, training or at least evaluating it on similarly informal text helps ensure realistic performance, rather than relying solely on clean, formal training data.

questions.question: Why can subword tokenization help with noisy, real-world text?
options: It can only process perfectly spelled words
It helps gracefully handle typos and unusual words better than pure word-level tokenization
It removes the need for any tokenization at all
It only works for formal news articles
questions.explanation: Subword tokenization can break unfamiliar or misspelled words into smaller recognizable pieces, making it more robust to the typos and unusual words common in noisy real-world text than pure word-level tokenization.

lessons.title: NLP Pitfalls and Ethical Considerations
lessons.description: Wrap up the course with a practical checklist of common mistakes and important ethical considerations in NLP.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can list common NLP pitfalls and describe key ethical considerations relevant to building language technology.

sections.title: 🧭 A recap of technical pitfalls from this course
sections.content:
• **Ignoring negation and context** — "not good" isn't the same as "good"
• **Assuming static embeddings capture full meaning** — they miss context-dependent meaning (module 5's contextual embeddings address this)
• **Trusting generated text (summaries, answers, translations) without verification** — the hallucination risk covered in module 4 applies broadly to any generative NLP task
• **Evaluating only on clean data** — real-world text is messier than benchmark datasets, as the previous lesson covered

sections.title: ⚖️ Bias in language models
sections.content:
Recall from module 2: embeddings and language models learn from real-world text, and real-world text contains real-world biases — stereotypical associations, imbalanced representation across demographic groups, and more. A model trained on biased data can reproduce (and sometimes amplify) that bias in its outputs, in ways that can cause real harm — like a resume-screening tool skewed by names associated with gender or ethnicity, or generated text that reinforces stereotypes.

This is an active area of ongoing research, without a single simple fix — but awareness is the essential first step: bias doesn't announce itself, it has to be specifically looked for through careful, deliberate evaluation.

sections.title: 🔒 Privacy and misuse considerations
sections.content:
• **Training data may contain personal or sensitive information** — text scraped from the web can include private details never intended for this kind of use
• **Generated text can be used to create convincing misinformation** — the same generation capabilities covered in this course (summarization, generative QA) can be misused to produce plausible-sounding but false content at scale
• **NER and similar techniques, while useful for legitimate purposes, could also enable unwanted surveillance or profiling** if applied without appropriate care and safeguards

Building NLP systems responsibly means actively considering these risks during design, not just treating them as someone else's problem to solve after the fact.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming bias is a rare edge case rather than a pervasive, structural risk.** Since embeddings and language models learn directly from real-world text, some degree of bias is the default outcome unless actively identified and addressed.

**Treating ethical considerations as separate from technical decisions.** Choices covered throughout this course — what data to train on, which evaluation examples to use, how to define "success" for a given task — are simultaneously technical and ethical decisions.

**Assuming these are someone else's problem to solve.** Anyone building or deploying NLP systems shares real responsibility for understanding and mitigating these risks, not just the researchers who first study them.

questions.question: Why can language models trained on real-world text end up exhibiting bias?
options: Language models are incapable of learning any patterns from data
Real-world text itself contains real-world biases and imbalanced representation, and models trained on it can absorb and reproduce those patterns
Bias only ever comes from the specific programming language used to build the model
This is not an actual concern for language models
questions.explanation: Since embeddings and language models learn purely from statistical patterns in their training text, any biases or imbalances present in that text (which reflects real-world societal patterns) can be absorbed into the model's learned associations and outputs.

questions.question: Why is it important to be cautious about generative NLP capabilities like summarization and generative QA from a misuse perspective?
options: These capabilities are only ever used for entirely benign purposes with no possible misuse
The same generation capabilities that produce useful summaries or answers could also be used to create convincing but false, misleading content at scale
Generative NLP techniques cannot actually produce readable text
Misuse is not a realistic concern for any NLP application
questions.explanation: The very capability that makes generative NLP useful — producing fluent, plausible-sounding text — is the same capability that could be misused to generate convincing misinformation at scale, which is why responsible development needs to consider this risk directly.

questions.question: What's the relationship between technical decisions (like choice of training data) and ethical considerations in NLP?
options: Technical decisions and ethical considerations are always completely separate and unrelated

Many technical decisions — like what data to train on or which examples to evaluate with — are simultaneously technical and ethical choices, since they directly shape a model's behavior and potential biases
Ethical considerations only apply after a model has already been fully deployed
There is no meaningful connection between the two
questions.explanation: Decisions like what data a model trains on, or which examples are used for evaluation, directly determine what patterns (including biases) a model learns — meaning these seemingly 'purely technical' choices carry real ethical weight and can't be neatly separated from ethical considerations.

questions.question: Why does a model trained on biased real-world text tend to reproduce that bias?
options: Models are immune to any bias present in their training data
Embeddings and language models learn from real-world text, and real-world text contains real-world biases and imbalanced representation
Bias only comes from the choice of programming language used
Bias is impossible to detect in any model
questions.explanation: Since these models learn purely from patterns in their training text, any biases or imbalances present in that text can be absorbed and reproduced in the model's outputs.

questions.question: What example does the lesson give of real-world harm from biased NLP models?
options: A spelling checker suggesting incorrect words
A resume-screening tool skewed by names associated with gender or ethnicity
A translation model taking too long to run
A summarization model producing overly long summaries
questions.explanation: The lesson specifically mentions a resume-screening tool skewed by names associated with gender or ethnicity as a real example of how bias in NLP models can cause tangible harm.

questions.question: What privacy concern does the lesson raise about training data?
options: Training data can never contain any personal information
Text scraped from the web can include private details never intended for this kind of use
Privacy is not a relevant concern for NLP systems
Training data is always manually reviewed for privacy before use
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that training data scraped from the web may contain personal or sensitive information that individuals never intended to be used this way.

questions.question: How could NER-like techniques be misused, according to the lesson?
options: They could never be misused under any circumstances
They could enable unwanted surveillance or profiling if applied without appropriate care and safeguards
NER techniques are only usable for translation tasks
Misuse of NER is purely a hypothetical concern with no real basis
questions.explanation: While useful for legitimate purposes, techniques like NER could enable unwanted surveillance or profiling of individuals if deployed without proper care and safeguards.

questions.question: According to the lesson, are ethical considerations in NLP separate from technical decisions?
options: Yes, they are entirely separate and unrelated
No — decisions like what data to train on and how to define success are simultaneously technical and ethical choices
Ethical considerations only matter after a model has been fully deployed
Technical decisions have no bearing on ethical outcomes
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that choices like training data selection and evaluation design are simultaneously technical and ethical decisions, since they directly shape a model's behavior and potential biases.
